molecules.name: Aspirin
molecules.use: Pain reliever and low-dose heart-attack prevention
molecules.fact: Aspirin blocks the COX enzyme in platelets, so they stop clumping for the rest of their 7 to 10 day life. That is why patients may be asked about aspirin before surgery or a tooth extraction. Old aspirin that smells like vinegar has had its ester hydrolyzed into acetic acid.

molecules.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
molecules.fact: Acetaminophen is broken down in the liver. In an overdose a toxic metabolite builds up and can destroy liver cells, so nurses watch total daily dose across combination products. The antidote is N-acetylcysteine.

molecules.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
molecules.use: NSAID for pain, fever and inflammation
molecules.fact: Ibuprofen lowers prostaglandins, which cause inflammation but also protect the stomach lining. That is why it is taken with food. It is one of the most common choices for dental pain after a procedure.

molecules.name: Naproxen (Aleve)
molecules.fact: Naproxen lasts longer than ibuprofen, so it is taken about every 12 hours instead of every 6 to 8. Like other NSAIDs, it can stress the kidneys and stomach.

molecules.name: Lidocaine
molecules.use: Local anesthetic (the classic dental numbing shot)
molecules.fact: Lidocaine blocks sodium channels in nerve cells, so pain signals (action potentials) cannot travel to the brain. Trick: amide anesthetics have two "i"s in the name (l-i-doca-i-ne) and are broken down by the liver.

molecules.name: Articaine
molecules.fact: Articaine is an amide anesthetic that also carries an ester. Enzymes in the blood quickly hydrolyze that ester, so it has a very short half-life in the body. That is one reason it is popular in dentistry.

molecules.name: Benzocaine (Orajel)
molecules.use: Topical numbing gel for gums and sore throats
molecules.fact: Benzocaine is an ester anesthetic used on the surface of the gums before an injection. The FDA warns against using it in children under 2 because it can cause methemoglobinemia, where blood cannot carry oxygen well.

molecules.name: Procaine (Novocain)
molecules.fact: Many people still call any dental shot "Novocain," but procaine is rarely used now. Ester anesthetics are hydrolyzed in the blood, and one breakdown product (PABA) causes allergies in some people.

molecules.name: Epinephrine (adrenaline)
molecules.fact: Epinephrine is made by the adrenal medulla. It is added to lidocaine dental cartridges because it constricts blood vessels, which keeps the anesthetic in place longer and reduces bleeding.

molecules.name: Dopamine
molecules.fact: Loss of dopamine-making neurons causes the tremor and stiffness of Parkinson's disease. Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so patients take L-DOPA, which the brain converts into dopamine.

molecules.name: Levodopa (L-DOPA)
molecules.fact: L-DOPA is an amino acid, so it can ride amino-acid transporters across the blood-brain barrier. High-protein meals compete for those transporters, so timing doses around meals matters.

molecules.name: Serotonin
molecules.use: Neurotransmitter for mood, sleep and gut movement
molecules.fact: About 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, not the brain. SSRI antidepressants such as fluoxetine keep more serotonin in the synapse.

molecules.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
molecules.fact: Diphenhydramine blocks histamine receptors. It crosses into the brain easily, which is why it causes drowsiness, and older adults are at higher risk of confusion and falls.

molecules.name: Morphine
molecules.fact: Opioids act on receptors in the brainstem that control breathing, so the biggest danger is respiratory depression. Nurses check respiratory rate and sedation before giving a dose.

molecules.name: Codeine
molecules.use: Mild opioid for pain and cough
molecules.fact: Codeine is morphine with its phenol turned into an ether. The liver enzyme CYP2D6 converts it back into morphine, and "ultra-rapid metabolizers" can make dangerous amounts, which is why it is no longer given to children.

molecules.name: Naloxone (Narcan)
molecules.fact: Naloxone fits the opioid receptor but does not activate it, pushing morphine-like drugs off. It can wear off before the opioid does, so the patient must be watched for breathing problems coming back.

molecules.name: Penicillin G
molecules.fact: The strained four-membered ring is a cyclic amide called a beta-lactam. It snaps open and jams the enzyme bacteria use to build their cell wall. Penicillin allergy is the most commonly reported drug allergy.

molecules.name: Amoxicillin
molecules.fact: Amoxicillin is the usual antibiotic given before dental work to patients with certain heart conditions, to prevent infective endocarditis. The extra amine group helps it absorb well when swallowed.

molecules.name: Glucose (open-chain form)
molecules.use: Main blood sugar and fuel for cells
molecules.fact: A normal fasting blood glucose is about 70 to 99 mg/dL. Insulin from the pancreas lets glucose into muscle and fat cells. The many OH groups make glucose very water soluble.

molecules.name: Fructose (open-chain form)
molecules.fact: Fructose is a ketose (sugar with a ketone), while glucose is an aldose (sugar with an aldehyde). Fructose is processed mostly by the liver.

molecules.name: Cholesterol
molecules.use: Membrane lipid and starting material for steroid hormones
molecules.fact: Your body builds cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, and vitamin D from cholesterol. The single OH makes one end slightly polar, so cholesterol tucks into cell membranes with the OH facing the water.

molecules.name: Testosterone
molecules.fact: Testosterone is made mainly by the testes and is a steroid, so it passes through cell membranes and binds receptors inside the cell.

molecules.name: Estradiol
molecules.fact: Estradiol is made mainly by the ovaries. Compare it with testosterone: the ketone ring has become an aromatic phenol ring. Estrogen also helps protect bone density, which is why bone loss speeds up after menopause.

molecules.name: Cortisol (hydrocortisone)
molecules.fact: Cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex. It raises blood glucose and calms inflammation. Long-term steroid medicines can suppress the body's own cortisol, so they are tapered instead of stopped suddenly.

molecules.name: Prednisone
molecules.use: Steroid for asthma flares and inflammation
molecules.fact: Prednisone is a prodrug: the liver reduces one of its ketones to an alcohol, making the active drug prednisolone. It is often used for asthma and COPD flare-ups.

molecules.name: Lactic acid
molecules.use: Made by muscles when oxygen is low
molecules.fact: When cells lack oxygen (sepsis, shock, intense exercise), pyruvate is converted to lactate. A high blood lactate level is a warning sign that tissues are not getting enough oxygen.

molecules.name: Pyruvic acid
molecules.fact: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvates. With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and the citric acid cycle. Without oxygen, it is reduced to lactic acid: the ketone becomes an alcohol.

molecules.name: Acetoacetic acid (a ketone body)
molecules.use: Ketone body made during fasting or diabetic ketoacidosis
molecules.fact: In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), the liver makes ketone bodies faster than the body can use them, and the blood becomes acidic. Some acetoacetic acid breaks down into acetone, giving the breath a fruity smell.

molecules.name: Citric acid
molecules.fact: Citrate is the first molecule of the citric acid cycle. Donated blood is stored with citrate, which binds calcium so blood cannot clot. Large transfusions can therefore lower a patient's calcium.

molecules.name: Acetylcholine
molecules.fact: Acetylcholine tells skeletal muscles to contract. The enzyme acetylcholinesterase ends the signal by hydrolyzing the ester. Nerve agents and some insecticides block that enzyme.

molecules.name: Urea
molecules.use: How the body gets rid of nitrogen
molecules.fact: The liver turns toxic ammonia into urea, and the kidneys excrete it. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is a routine lab test of kidney function. Urea is also in carbamide peroxide teeth-whitening gels.

molecules.name: Glycylalanine (a dipeptide)
molecules.use: Two amino acids joined by a peptide bond
molecules.fact: A peptide bond is an amide. Every protein, from collagen in your gums to hemoglobin in your blood, is a long chain of these amide links. Proteins always have a free amine at one end and a free carboxylic acid at the other.

molecules.name: Aspartame (NutraSweet)
molecules.fact: Mouth bacteria cannot ferment aspartame, so it does not cause cavities. In the body the ester and amide are hydrolyzed, releasing phenylalanine, which is why products carry a warning for people with PKU.

molecules.name: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
molecules.fact: Without vitamin C, the body cannot make strong collagen. Scurvy causes swollen, bleeding gums and loose teeth. The ring is a cyclic ester (a lactone).

molecules.name: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
molecules.fact: Fluoxetine and its breakdown product stay in the body for days to weeks, longer than most antidepressants. Drug designers often add C–F bonds (like this CF3) because they resist being broken down. Mood effects usually take a few weeks to appear.

molecules.name: Sevoflurane
molecules.fact: Sevoflurane has a sweet smell and does not irritate the airway, so it is used to put children to sleep by mask. It is a small ether covered in fluorine atoms.

molecules.name: Isoflurane
molecules.fact: Isoflurane is a halogenated ether. Its pungent smell can make patients cough, so it is usually started after the patient is already asleep.

molecules.name: Salicylic acid
molecules.use: Acne and wart treatments; what aspirin turns into
molecules.fact: Willow bark has been used for pain for thousands of years because it contains a relative of salicylic acid. Aspirin was made by turning the phenol into an ester so it is gentler on the stomach.

molecules.name: Methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen)
molecules.fact: Methyl salicylate gives Bengay and some mouthwashes their wintergreen smell. It is absorbed through skin and is toxic if swallowed in large amounts, especially by children.

molecules.name: Eugenol (clove oil)
molecules.use: Dental sedative dressings and temporary fillings
molecules.fact: Mixed with zinc oxide, eugenol makes zinc oxide-eugenol (ZOE), used for temporary fillings and dry-socket dressings. It soothes irritated pulp and has mild antibacterial action.

molecules.name: Xylitol
molecules.fact: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol. The cavity bacterium Streptococcus mutans cannot use it for energy, so chewing xylitol gum can reduce cavity risk. It is very toxic to dogs.

molecules.name: Albuterol
molecules.fact: Albuterol activates beta-2 receptors that relax the smooth muscle around the airways. Compare it with epinephrine: the bulky tert-butyl group on the nitrogen makes it more selective for the lungs. A fast heartbeat and shakiness are common side effects.

molecules.name: Atropine
molecules.use: Speeds a slow heart rate; dries secretions
molecules.fact: Atropine blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. It speeds up the heart and reduces saliva and airway secretions, which is why it has been used before surgery and some dental procedures.

molecules.name: Warfarin (Coumadin)
molecules.fact: Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K, which the liver needs to make clotting factors. Patients get regular INR blood tests, and dental teams check the INR before extractions.

molecules.name: Phenylephrine
molecules.fact: Phenylephrine squeezes blood vessels (alpha-1 receptors). IV, it raises blood pressure. Taken as a pill for a stuffy nose, an FDA panel concluded in 2023 that it does not work, because the liver breaks most of it down first.

molecules.name: Capsaicin
molecules.use: Chili pepper heat; topical pain cream
molecules.fact: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 heat-pain receptor, so your nerves report "burning" even though nothing is hot. Repeated use makes those nerve endings less sensitive, which is how capsaicin creams relieve pain.

molecules.name: Cinnamaldehyde
molecules.use: Cinnamon flavor in gum and toothpaste
molecules.fact: Cinnamon-flavored gum and toothpaste can cause an allergic reaction inside the mouth (cinnamon contact stomatitis), with red, sore or white patches that clear up when the product is stopped.

molecules.name: Retinal
molecules.use: The light-catching molecule in your eye
molecules.fact: In the rods of your retina, light flips one C=C double bond of retinal from cis to trans, which triggers a nerve signal. Retinal comes from vitamin A, so vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.

molecules.name: Glutaraldehyde
molecules.fact: Glutaraldehyde has two aldehyde groups that cross-link proteins, which kills bacteria, viruses and spores. It is used to disinfect heat-sensitive equipment such as endoscopes, and it is irritating to skin and lungs.

molecules.name: Propofol
molecules.fact: Propofol is so water-insoluble (big nonpolar groups around one phenol) that it is given as a milky white oil-in-water emulsion, earning the nickname "milk of amnesia."

molecules.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
molecules.fact: Oseltamivir is a prodrug: the liver hydrolyzes its ester into a carboxylic acid, the active form that blocks the flu enzyme neuraminidase. It works best if started within 48 hours of symptoms.

molecules.name: Thyroxine (T4, levothyroxine)
molecules.fact: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make this hormone, which is why table salt is iodized. Levothyroxine pills are taken on an empty stomach, because food and calcium reduce absorption.

molecules.name: Nicotine
molecules.fact: Nicotine constricts blood vessels and reduces blood flow to the gums, which can hide the bleeding that usually signals gum disease. Smokers have a much higher risk of periodontal disease.

molecules.name: Menthol
molecules.use: Cooling flavor in toothpaste, lozenges and rubs
molecules.fact: Menthol does not lower temperature. It activates the TRPM8 cold receptor, so nerves report "cool." It is a cyclic alcohol.

molecules.name: Triclosan
molecules.use: Antibacterial once found in toothpaste and soap
molecules.fact: The FDA banned triclosan from consumer antibacterial hand soaps in 2016, and the main toothpaste that used it was reformulated without it in 2019.

molecules.name: Glycerol (glycerin)
molecules.use: Backbone of fats; moisturizer in toothpaste
molecules.fact: Glycerol forms the backbone of triglycerides: each OH becomes an ester with a fatty acid. In toothpaste it keeps the paste from drying out.

molecules.name: Tranexamic acid
molecules.use: Stops bleeding by protecting blood clots
molecules.fact: Tranexamic acid blocks the enzyme that breaks down clots. It is used for trauma, heavy menstrual bleeding, and as a mouth rinse after extractions in patients with bleeding disorders.

molecules.name: Metoprolol
molecules.use: Beta blocker for blood pressure and heart rate
molecules.fact: Beta blockers end in "-olol." They slow the heart, so nurses check the apical pulse and blood pressure before giving a dose and may hold it if the heart rate is too low.

molecules.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
molecules.fact: Furosemide works in the loop of Henle in the kidney, making the body lose sodium and water. It also flushes out potassium, so potassium levels are monitored.

molecules.name: Oleic acid
molecules.use: Main fatty acid in olive oil
molecules.fact: Oleic acid has one cis C=C, which puts a kink in the chain. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, so fats rich in oleic acid are liquid oils at room temperature.

molecules.name: Iohexol (Omnipaque)
molecules.use: Iodinated contrast dye for CT scans and X-rays
molecules.fact: Iodine atoms have many electrons and absorb X-rays strongly, so blood vessels filled with contrast show up bright. All those OH and amide groups make the molecule very water soluble so it can be injected and cleared by the kidneys.

molecules.name: Fludeoxyglucose (FDG)
molecules.fact: FDG is glucose with one OH swapped for radioactive fluorine-18. Cancer cells take up glucose quickly, so they glow on a PET scan. It cannot finish glycolysis, so it gets trapped inside the cells.

molecules.name: Ethyl chloride
molecules.fact: Ethyl chloride boils at about 12 °C. Sprayed on the skin, it evaporates almost instantly and absorbs heat, numbing the area for a quick injection or IV start.

molecules.name: Isopropyl alcohol
molecules.use: Rubbing alcohol for skin and surface disinfection
molecules.fact: 70% isopropyl alcohol kills germs better than 99%, because the water helps it get into cells and denature proteins and slows evaporation so it stays on the surface longer.

molecules.name: Phenol (carbolic acid)
molecules.fact: In 1867 Joseph Lister started spraying phenol in the operating room and surgical infections dropped sharply. Today about 1.4% phenol is the numbing ingredient in Chloraseptic throat spray. An OH on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol.

molecules.name: Toluene (methylbenzene)
molecules.use: Solvent in paints, glues and nail polish
molecules.fact: The liver oxidizes toluene's CH3 into a COOH, making benzoic acid, which is then excreted in urine as hippuric acid. Urine hippuric acid has been used to check workers for toluene exposure. A methyl group is not a functional group, so toluene is just an aromatic hydrocarbon.

molecules.name: Anisole (methoxybenzene)
molecules.fact: Anisole is phenol with the H on the oxygen replaced by CH3. Without that O–H it cannot hydrogen bond to itself, so it boils at about 154 °C, compared with about 182 °C for phenol.

molecules.name: Benzoic acid
molecules.use: Food and medicine preservative (as sodium benzoate)
molecules.fact: Sodium benzoate keeps many liquid medicines and sodas from spoiling. The body attaches glycine to benzoic acid to make hippuric acid, which carries nitrogen out in urine. Doctors use that trick to treat some urea-cycle disorders.

molecules.name: Benzaldehyde
molecules.fact: Benzaldehyde gives cherry-flavored liquid medicines their taste. Left open to air, it slowly oxidizes into benzoic acid (aldehyde → carboxylic acid), and white crystals form around the bottle cap.

molecules.name: Acetophenone
molecules.use: The simplest aromatic ketone; fragrance ingredient
molecules.fact: In the 1880s acetophenone was sold as a sleeping medicine called "Hypnone." It was abandoned, but its ketone sits next to the benzene ring the same way it does in many modern drugs.

molecules.name: Aniline
molecules.use: Starting material for dyes and drugs
molecules.fact: Aniline exposure can cause methemoglobinemia, where blood turns chocolate-brown and cannot carry oxygen well. Turning aniline's amine into an amide gave acetanilide, an early fever reducer that led to acetaminophen.

molecules.name: Acetanilide (Antifebrin)
molecules.use: One of the first synthetic fever reducers (1886)
molecules.fact: A pharmacy accidentally gave acetanilide to a patient in 1886, and it lowered the fever. It was too toxic for long-term use, but adding an OH to the ring led to acetaminophen. Compare the two: same amide, plus a phenol.

molecules.name: Chlorobenzene
molecules.fact: A halogen attached to a benzene ring shows up in many drugs: chlorine in diazepam and ketamine, fluorine in midazolam. Halogens make molecules more fat soluble, helping drugs reach the brain.

molecules.name: Benzyl alcohol
molecules.use: Preservative in bacteriostatic saline and multi-dose vials
molecules.fact: Benzyl alcohol keeps multi-dose vials sterile, but newborns cannot break it down well, and it caused "gasping syndrome" in premature babies. That is why preservative-free saline is used for neonates. The OH is on a CH2, not the ring, so this is an alcohol, not a phenol.

molecules.name: Styrene (vinylbenzene)
molecules.fact: The C=C double bonds of styrene molecules link end to end to make polystyrene, used in foam cups and many disposable lab and medical trays. This is the same alkene addition chemistry used to set dental resins.

molecules.name: m-Cresol
molecules.use: Preservative in insulin vials and pens
molecules.fact: m-Cresol keeps multi-dose insulin sterile after the stopper has been punctured. It is also what gives insulin its "bandage" smell. It is a phenol with a methyl group on the ring.

molecules.name: Thymol
molecules.fact: Listerine's essential oils are thymol, eucalyptol, menthol, and methyl salicylate. They disrupt bacterial cell membranes in plaque biofilm. Thymol comes from the herb thyme.

molecules.name: Hydroquinone
molecules.fact: Hydroquinone blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts making melanin pigment. It is easily oxidized, which is also why it was used as a photographic developer.

molecules.name: Benzyl benzoate
molecules.fact: Benzyl benzoate is an ester made from benzoic acid and benzyl alcohol. It is toxic to the mites that cause scabies. Try naming its two halves: the alcohol part comes first ("benzyl"), then the acid part ("benzoate").

molecules.name: Guaifenesin (Mucinex)
molecules.fact: Guaifenesin is meant to thin mucus so it is easier to cough up. It is a cousin of guaiacol, a compound from wood tar used in cough remedies since the 1800s.

molecules.name: Vanillin
molecules.use: Vanilla flavor in foods and chewable medicines
molecules.fact: Vanillin packs three groups onto one benzene ring: an aldehyde, an ether, and a phenol. It is one of the most widely used flavorings for masking bitter medicines.

molecules.name: Phenylalanine
molecules.fact: In phenylketonuria (PKU), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine does not work. Phenylalanine builds up and can damage the brain, so newborns are screened at birth.

molecules.name: Tyrosine
molecules.use: Amino acid that becomes hormones and pigment
molecules.fact: Tyrosine is the starting point for dopamine, epinephrine, thyroid hormones, and melanin. Its phenol OH is what makes it different from phenylalanine.

molecules.name: Ethinyl estradiol
molecules.use: Estrogen in most combined birth-control pills
molecules.fact: Adding a C≡C (alkyne) next to the OH blocks the liver from breaking the molecule down, so it works when swallowed. Estrogen raises clotting factors, which is why smokers over 35 are advised against combined pills.

molecules.name: Prilocaine (Citanest)
molecules.fact: The liver breaks prilocaine down into o-toluidine, which can cause methemoglobinemia at high doses. Prilocaine is avoided in patients already at risk for that condition.

molecules.name: Mepivacaine (Carbocaine)
molecules.use: Dental local anesthetic, often used without epinephrine
molecules.fact: Mepivacaine widens blood vessels less than most local anesthetics, so the 3% "plain" version works without epinephrine. That makes it useful for short procedures and patients who should limit epinephrine.

molecules.name: Bupivacaine (Marcaine)
molecules.fact: The longer butyl chain makes bupivacaine more fat soluble, so it stays in nerve membranes for many hours. It is used for long surgeries and post-op pain control, but it is the most toxic to the heart if it reaches the blood in high amounts.

molecules.name: Tetracaine
molecules.use: Topical ester anesthetic (eye drops, nasal dental spray)
molecules.fact: Tetracaine is in Kovanaze, a nasal spray that numbs upper teeth without a needle. Like other ester anesthetics, it is broken down in the blood by pseudocholinesterase.

molecules.name: Methyl methacrylate
molecules.use: Monomer for dentures, retainers and bone cement
molecules.fact: When methyl methacrylate polymerizes, its C=C double bonds link up into the hard acrylic (PMMA) of denture bases, orthodontic retainers, and custom trays. The liquid monomer has a strong odor and can irritate skin.

molecules.name: HEMA (2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate)
molecules.fact: HEMA helps bonding agents soak into dentin. Its small size lets it pass through many glove materials within minutes, making it a common cause of allergic skin reactions in dental staff.

molecules.name: Bis-GMA
molecules.use: Main resin in composite fillings and sealants
molecules.fact: Bis-GMA has a reactive C=C at each end. When the blue curing light starts polymerization, those alkenes link many molecules into a hard network, which is how sealants and composite fillings set.

molecules.name: Camphorquinone
molecules.fact: Camphorquinone absorbs blue light around 470 nm, the color of a dental curing light, and kicks off polymerization. Its two ketone groups are also why uncured composite has a slight yellow tint.

molecules.name: Eucalyptol
molecules.fact: Eucalyptol is one of the four essential oils in Listerine. In endodontics it is used as a solvent to soften gutta-percha when a root canal needs to be redone.

molecules.name: Tetracycline
molecules.fact: Tetracyclines bind calcium in teeth that are still forming, leaving permanent gray-brown stains. They are generally avoided in pregnancy and in children under 8. A low dose of doxycycline, a relative, is used to treat periodontitis.

molecules.name: Hydrocodone
molecules.fact: Hydrocodone is codeine with its alcohol oxidized to a ketone and its C=C reduced to a single bond. Current dental guidelines recommend ibuprofen with acetaminophen first for tooth-extraction pain, keeping opioids for cases where that is not enough.

molecules.name: Diazepam (Valium)
molecules.fact: Diazepam may be prescribed before a dental visit for very anxious patients, who then need someone to drive them home. Benzodiazepine sedation can be reversed with flumazenil.

molecules.name: Midazolam (Versed)
molecules.fact: Midazolam works fast, wears off quickly, and usually causes amnesia, so patients often do not remember the procedure. Breathing and oxygen levels are monitored during sedation.

molecules.name: Ketamine
molecules.fact: Unlike most anesthetics, ketamine usually keeps breathing and airway reflexes working, which makes it useful in emergencies and in the field. A related form is now approved as a nasal spray for depression.

molecules.name: Fentanyl
molecules.use: Very potent opioid for anesthesia and severe pain
molecules.fact: Fentanyl is roughly 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine, so doses are in micrograms. It is used during anesthesia and in skin patches, and naloxone reverses it.

molecules.name: Succinylcholine
molecules.fact: Succinylcholine is basically two acetylcholine molecules joined together. Blood pseudocholinesterase hydrolyzes its esters within minutes, but people with a genetic deficiency of that enzyme can stay paralyzed for hours.

molecules.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
molecules.fact: Since 2006, US law has kept pseudoephedrine behind the pharmacy counter with ID required, because it can be chemically converted into methamphetamine. It also raises blood pressure and heart rate.

molecules.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
molecules.fact: Skin makes vitamin D when UVB light breaks open one ring of a cholesterol-derived molecule. Without enough vitamin D, the gut absorbs less calcium, weakening bones and developing teeth.

molecules.name: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol)
molecules.fact: Vitamin E's long carbon tail anchors it inside cell membranes, while its phenol OH gives up a hydrogen atom to stop free radicals from damaging the membrane's fatty acids.

molecules.name: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P)
molecules.use: 3-carbon sugar in the middle of glycolysis
molecules.fact: Glycolysis splits a 6-carbon sugar into two 3-carbon pieces. When G3P's aldehyde is oxidized, NAD⁺ picks up electrons to become NADH, one of the energy payoffs of glycolysis. (The –OPO₃H₂ group is a phosphate, not one of our labeled groups.)

molecules.name: Dihydroxyacetone (DHA)
molecules.use: Glycolysis partner of G3P; sunless tanning ingredient
molecules.fact: DHA (as its phosphate) is the ketone partner of G3P in glycolysis, and an enzyme flips one into the other. On skin, DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer, which is how sunless tanning lotions turn skin brown.

molecules.name: β-Hydroxybutyric acid
molecules.use: Main "ketone body" in fasting and DKA
molecules.fact: β-Hydroxybutyrate is the most abundant ketone body in diabetic ketoacidosis and is what hospital blood ketone tests usually measure. Surprise: it has no ketone group at all. It is an alcohol plus a carboxylic acid, made by reducing acetoacetic acid.

molecules.name: Acetone
molecules.fact: Acetoacetic acid slowly loses CO₂ to form acetone, which is breathed out. That is the fruity or nail-polish smell on the breath of a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis.

molecules.name: Succinic acid
molecules.fact: Succinate dehydrogenase removes two H atoms from succinate to make fumarate, creating a C=C. That enzyme is also Complex II of the electron transport chain, linking the Krebs cycle directly to ATP production.

molecules.name: Fumaric acid
molecules.fact: In the Krebs cycle, water adds across fumarate's C=C to make malate. That is the same hydration reaction (alkene + H₂O → alcohol) you learn in CHEM 3B.

molecules.name: Malic acid
molecules.use: Krebs cycle intermediate; sour taste of apples
molecules.fact: Malate's secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, making oxaloacetate and producing NADH. That is the CHEM 3B rule "2° alcohol → ketone" happening in your mitochondria.

molecules.name: Oxaloacetic acid
molecules.fact: Oxaloacetate joins acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) to make citrate (6 carbons), starting each turn of the Krebs cycle. In the liver it is also a starting point for making new glucose (gluconeogenesis).

molecules.name: Isocitric acid
molecules.fact: Citrate is rearranged into isocitrate so its OH sits on a secondary carbon. That 2° alcohol can then be oxidized to a ketone, and the molecule loses CO₂, one of the steps where you make the CO₂ you exhale.

molecules.name: α-Ketoglutaric acid
molecules.fact: In transamination, α-ketoglutarate takes the amine group from an amino acid and becomes glutamate. The liver enzymes ALT and AST on a lab panel are transamination enzymes, so high blood levels signal liver damage.

molecules.name: Glutamic acid (glutamate)
molecules.fact: Glutamate is the brain's main "go" signal and the flavor in MSG (umami). It carries nitrogen collected from other amino acids to the liver, where it is ultimately turned into urea.

molecules.name: Alanine
molecules.use: Amino acid that shuttles between muscle and liver
molecules.fact: Swap alanine's amine for a C=O and you get pyruvate. ALT (alanine aminotransferase) does exactly that, and its blood level is a standard liver test.

molecules.name: GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid)
molecules.fact: GABA is made from glutamate by removing CO₂. Benzodiazepines like diazepam and midazolam make GABA receptors work harder, which is why they calm anxiety and cause drowsiness.

molecules.name: Acetaldehyde (ethanal)
molecules.fact: The liver oxidizes ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid (alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid). Acetaldehyde causes flushing, nausea and headache. The drug disulfiram blocks the second step on purpose, so drinking makes people feel sick.

molecules.name: Ethanol
molecules.fact: The liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, and nothing (coffee, cold showers) speeds that up much. The first step is oxidation of the 1° alcohol to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase.

molecules.name: Methanol
molecules.fact: Methanol itself is not very toxic, but the liver oxidizes it to formaldehyde and then formic acid, which can cause blindness and acidosis. The antidote fomepizole blocks that first oxidation step.

molecules.name: Palmitic acid
molecules.fact: Beta-oxidation chops fatty acids into 2-carbon acetyl-CoA pieces, so 16-carbon palmitic acid yields 8 acetyl-CoA. Gram for gram, fat stores more than twice the energy of carbohydrate (9 vs 4 Calories per gram).

molecules.name: Tributyrin (a triglyceride)
molecules.fact: A triglyceride is glycerol with all three OH groups turned into esters. Lipase enzymes from the pancreas hydrolyze those esters, releasing glycerol and three fatty acids that the intestine can absorb.

molecules.name: Creatinine
molecules.use: Waste product used to check kidney function
molecules.fact: Muscles turn creatine into creatinine at a fairly steady rate, and healthy kidneys filter it out. Serum creatinine (and the eGFR calculated from it) is one of the most common kidney lab tests, checked before giving contrast dye or kidney-cleared drugs.

molecules.name: Uric acid
molecules.use: End product of purine (DNA/RNA base) breakdown
molecules.fact: When uric acid builds up, it crystallizes in joints (often the big toe), causing gout. Allopurinol treats gout by blocking the enzyme that makes uric acid.
